newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu-Kabila to meet for Zaire peace talks, U.N..
newsitem.headline: Mobutu-Kabila to meet for Zaire peace talks, U.N..

text.p: Zaire civil war foes President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila have agreed in principle to meet to prepare the way for elections, U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said on Thursday.
Sahnoun and South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said in a joint statement President Nelson Mandela had formally invited Mobutu to meet Kabila in South Africa "as early as possible".

"We are confident that a meeting will be held soon and will discuss transitional arrangements affecting all elements of government in the context of a peaceful and negotiated solution (to the civil war)," they said in the statement.

"With all the legacies that are there, the outcome that we have today (is) the agreement of the two parties to meet at the highest level. I think it is a remarkable achievement," said Sahnoun, an Algerian diplomat.

Sahnoun, who is also the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) representative for Zaire, added during a news conference that the two sides had agreed in principle to meet during proximity talks in Cape Town on Wednesday involving Kabila and Mobutu envoy Honore Ngbanda.
Ngbanda left on a South African aircraft with an invitation from Mandela to Mobutu and a separate jet flew Kabila back to Lubumbashi, the mining centre taken last week by the rebels.
Sahnoun said the transitional arrangements referred to in the statement were intended to lead to democratic elections in the country ruled by Mobutu for 32 years.

Pahad, who, with South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki has played a key role in bringing the two sides to the brink of direct talks, said he was confident that substantive negotiations would begin soon.
"The fact of the commitment is there now. It's just a matter of setting up the detailed arrangements. We are confident that both parties are seeking a solution," he said.

Pahad said the two sides agreed to the talks without preconditions. Mobutu had previously insisted that a ceasefire should precede negotiations and Kabila has said there will be no ceasefire until Mobutu steps down.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) has conquered about half of the vast Central African country since October.
Mandela spent an hour talking to Kabila on Wednesday in what a government source said was a crucial meeting to persuade Kabila to drop his insistence on Mobutu's resignation.

"I have been speaking both to (rebel) president Kabila and to President Mobutu and as a result of the exchanges... I am confident that a peaceful solution will be achieved," Mandela told reporters on Thursday.
Mandela said he had spoken to Mobutu three times since last Saturday.
"He is very cooperative, but what he is going to do eventually I cannot predict. I believe he, himself, has an interest in a negotiated settement," Mandela added.
A government source said Mandela was trying to steer the two sides toward a settlement that included all factions claiming power or influence in Zaire.
"The important thing for the president is that nobody should be left out... he wants a coalition that leaves nobody on the outside," the source said.

In Kinshasa, Zaire's radical opposition demanded a seat at any talks between Mobutu and Kabila, with powerful opposition member of parliament Andre Boboliko saying the populist former prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi was entitled to join the talks because of a long campaign for democracy.

The Swiss government on Thursday rejected demands by Zairean rebels and Swiss politicians that it freeze billions of dollars Mobutu may have deposited in Swiss banks. The cabinet said Mobutu was still head of state.
